candidates.core_provocation: At a hospital where memories can be transferred but not copied, a dying father asks his wife to give him her last memory of their daughter so he can recognize the girl before he dies. After the procedure, he remembers that his wife—not the illness—killed their daughter, even though the memory seems to describe a crime that has not happened yet.
candidates.why_interesting: The story turns a tender act of memory-sharing into a race to discover whether the memory is a warning, a lie, or the future.

candidates.core_provocation: A man wakes in a hospital with two complete and incompatible sets of memories: one says he is the patient in the bed, while the other says he is the surgeon standing beside it. The hospital calls one set a corrupted backup, but the surgeon-memory tells him that choosing the wrong identity will result in his death.
candidates.why_interesting: The reader must keep questioning which memories are real while the protagonist has only minutes to make a terrifying choice.

candidates.core_provocation: At a hospital that removes traumatic memories and stores them as legal evidence, a nurse discovers a sealed recording labeled with her own name. It shows her killing a patient who is still alive—and when she asks him about it, he says the hospital is preparing to make the memory come true.
candidates.why_interesting: A supposedly reliable memory becomes a countdown to a crime, reversing the usual question of whether the past can be trusted into whether the future can be remembered.

parsed.reason_for_choice: The third idea offers the clearest short-story engine: a concrete mystery, a hospital deadline, and immediate personal danger. Its reversal naturally drives the plot forward as the nurse tries to prevent—or understand—the crime she has already seen.
